claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element, nearly equiatomic automotive alloy.
Active metals are dispersed in a homogeneous matrix in the starting catalyst.
A low-temperature hydrogen reduction pretreatment will form finely dispersed sub-nanometer metallic clusters at the catalyst surface.
The pretreatment should use 5–10 vol% H2 in N2 at approximately 200 °C for 1–2 hours.
The surface clusters are expected to include active platinum-group metals such as Pt or Pd.
Cluster formation will be accompanied by a modified electronic structure that stabilizes active interfaces within the multi-element matrix.
The reductive environment promotes surface segregation of the most active elements into well-dispersed clusters.
The surrounding alloy matrix prevents the segregated clusters from sintering.
The tailored surface structure enhances catalytic turnover.
The tailored surface structure resists poisoning by H2O and NO.
Hydrogen pretreatment will produce significantly higher low-temperature conversion than the untreated catalyst.
Hydrogen pretreatment will reduce deactivation during exposure to H2O and NO relative to the untreated catalyst.
Hydrogen pretreatment will improve stability after prolonged thermal cycling relative to the untreated catalyst.
The intervention will maintain low platinum-group-metal consumption.
The untreated catalyst typically suffers activity loss and durability limitations under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The expected improvement is bounded to the specified reduction treatment and an operating range of approximately 200–300 °C.
Poor control of reduction parameters may cause over-reduction or sintering and compromise catalyst performance.
